[912 F] (iii) The evidence regarding the injuries caused by the accused was not reliable. [913 G] (iv) The evidence about the assault on the deceased was not reliable as there was no previous enmity between the parties. [914 H] (v) The evidence relating to the assault on Ramchander was not reliable because he was not present at the scene of occurrence. [915 B C] (vi) There is nothing in the evidence to show that the accused or the eye witnesses were present at the time of the assault. 232: The respondent was charged with various offences under the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949, and was convicted by the Special Court established thereunder. He was sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment on conviction but he was acquitted in appeal by the High Court. On revision, the High Court set aside the conviction and directed that the case be sent back for trial to the special court constituted under section 5 (1) of the Act. The State Government filed an application before the High Court for a direction to the Special Court to try the case as a sessions case. The High Court held that the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure for trial of warrant cases by the Magistrate, trial without jury or assessors, restriction of the court 's power in granting adjournments, special powers to deal with refractory accused and dispensation of de novo trial on transfer of a case from one special court to another, and that the provisions of section 5(1) were discriminatory in so far as it authorised the State Government to direct that certain offences or classes of offences or classes or cases should be tried by a special court. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) Section 5(1), which is in the nature of a proviso, provides that nothing in sub section (2) shall apply to any offence triable by a special judge. It does not provide that the special judge must have been given the same powers as the ordinary courts of criminal justice. [550 C] (ii)The proviso to section 5(2) makes it clear that the special Judge can take cognizance of any offence without the previous sanction of the State Government. The proviso gives the State Government the power to authorise the special judge to take cognizance of such offence without the prior approval of the State government. The proviso does not confer upon the State Government any such power. The proviso merely confers upon the State government the power to appoint a special judge for trying a particular case. The State government has the power to remove the special judge and appoint another special judge. The State legislature cannot delegate its power to the special judge. [553 D E]

They did not disclose the fact that the awards in question were made within the specified time. The petitioners were aware of the fact that they would be entitled to the benefit of the award. 7130: The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and injunction filed by the respondents. They claimed that they had been in possession of the suit property since the time of their father, who was a tenant under the appellants. The suit was dismissed on the ground that the plaintiffs were not in lawful possession of the property. The Trial Court decreed the suit. On appeal the Appellate Court reversed the decree holding that the plaintiffs had been in lawful possession since the time when the lease stood terminated by efflux of time and the defendants were entitled to let out the property to the defendant No. 1. The High Court held that the plaintiffs could not be dispossessed from the suit property without resorting to the provisions of the Act. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by res judicata as well as constructive res judicata as found in Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in dismissing the suit. [1020F] (2) The High court was wrong in holding that the suit is barred by res judcia l law. [1021A] (3) The High Courts have consistently taken the view that the rights of the parties are governed by the terms of the contract between the parties and the courts have no jurisdiction to decide any question which arises out of the contract. [1022B] (4) The High courts have consistently taken a contrary view. [1023C] (5) The High has rightly held that the suit for eviction was maintainable. [1024D] (6) The High was right in holding that there was no bar against the maintainability of the suit. The High court erred in holding that it was open to the appellants to file a fresh suit after the expiry of the lease. [1025E] (7) The High should have considered whether the suit was within the period of limitation or not. [1026G]
6270: The respondent was appointed as Secretary, Zila Sainik Board, Unnao on 20th August, 1979. He was allowed to continue in service till 30th of August, 1985 and he was paid salary upto the period he was entitled to remain in service. On 29th September, 1981, the State Government issued an order extending the term of the respondent as Secretary, District Sainiks Board, Unnayan, Unnaon for a further period of one year with effect from 1st October, 1982. The respondent filed a Review Petition before the High Court contending that he was enti tled to be reinstated in service on the pronouncement of the Judgment by this Court in Civil Appeal No. 622 of 1987. The High Court dismissed the review petition holding that the respondent was not entitled to be reinstated into service on the basis of the interim order dated 10th July, 1986 passed by this Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the circumstances, it is open for the respondent to consider the claim of the respondent for continuation in service or of fresh appointment and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. [243C] 1.2 The respondent had not urged before the High court that the order of extension of his term was illegal or improper. 715: The appellant No. 1 was dismissed from service by the Chief Presidency Magistrate on January 17, 1952. He filed a complaint in the Court of the Chief Presidency magistrate against the two appellants and the partners of the appellant No. I for offences under sections 33 read with section 31 of the , and section 31(1) (b) of the Act. The Chief Presidency Magistrate acquitted all the accused including the appellants and held that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17,1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the accused persons could not be convicted under section 31(i) of the ,and section 31(2)(b) of Act. The High Court set aside the order of acquittal passed by the Chief committing Magistrate and held that the conciliation proceedings should be terminated when the report under section 12(6) is made by the Conciliation Officer within the time prescribed by the Act. Held, that the provisions of section 12( 6) of the . , are mandatory and they do not confer any right upon the person who has been dismissed or discharged from his employment. The assessee was the sole proprietor of certain lands situated within the limits of the village of Benarasi. The income from these lands was received by the assessee as an allowance during the previous year of the assessment year 1949 50. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the sum of Rs. 36,396/ received by the appellant was agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Income tax Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the amount of Rs.36,396/- was not agricultural income but was a part of the estate of the assessee. The High Court on reference, held that the receipt of Rs. 37,396 / was agricultural income and that it fell within the definition of agricultural income under section 2(i) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The expression "agricultural income" has been used in the context of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and the word "income" in the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. [173 G] (2) The expression 'agricultural income' has been defined in section 2(5) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 and it includes agricultural income derived from land which is used for agricultural purposes. [174 B C] (3) The expression agricultural income means agricultural income derived directly or indirectly from sources specified in the Schedule. It does not include agricultural income derived by way of rent. [175 D] (4) The expression income derived from property ordinarily connotes the idea of direct and immediate source of income. The expression "income", therefore, cannot be confined only to income derived from agriculture. [177 E] (5) The expression has been used to describe the income derived from the property ordinarily used for agricultural purpose. The expression has also been used to denote the income derived by the assessee from the property which is used exclusively for agricultural purposes and not by directly extending it to cases where the revenue or part thereof changes hands either by way of distribution of dividends or otherwise.

2593: The appellant was a Government servant in the State of Bombay. He was dismissed from service by an order dated February 2, 1955. The power conferred on the Governor under article 311(1) is not absolute and it can be exercised only in certain circumstances and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed or provided by rules made under the proviso to article 309. The power to dismiss a government servant is vested in the highest authority in the State and the same can be exercised either by way of punishment or by way of penalty. It cannot be said that the power to dismiss the government servant was taken away by the terms of the article and the High Court was right in holding that the order of termination of services of the appellant was illegal. The power of dismissing a government servant could be exercised only by way of imposing some other conditions which were not necessary for the exercise of the power. The power was not intended to be used to punish the government servant but to make him workable. The power could be exercised even in respect of matters falling within the purview of the executive power of the State. The power must be exercised in accordance with the rules made under section 49 of the Act. The power is not absolute. The power has to be exercised in conformity with the rules framed under section 49. The rule making authority did not have the power to prescribe any particular form of procedure for the exercise thereof. The rulemaking authority had no power to prescribe the manner in which the powers are to be exercised. The rule-making authority had the power to fix the period of probation of the government servants and the rules made thereunder. The rules made under sections 49 and 49A of the Act were not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act and were therefore invalid. The rule prescribing the period of service was not inconsistent with any of the provisions of Part III of the Constitution and was not saved by article 311(3). 1789: The appellant Company was incorporated in the year 1959 under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 55. 3356: The accused was charged under section 302/34 IPC for murdering the deceased. The evidence does not suffer from any infirmity. [705 E] 5. The evidence is not such as would render it unreliable. [706 F] 6. The evidence in the instant case is not so much about the actual assault on the deceased but is more about the manner in which the incident took place. It is true that the evidence is not so very convincing as to throw light on the question whether the accused persons were armed with deadly weapons or whether they were armed with knives. The appellant was charged with having murdered one of his employees, who was then working as a clerk in the Buland Shahar Post Office. The Additional Sessions judge acquitted the appellant but convicted him for offences under sections 52 and 467 of the Indian Penal Code. In appeal the High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letter was recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives the greatest that could be said is that he was in possession of the articles, and (2) that the prosecution having only shown that the appellant was in possession, there was no prejudice. HELD: (i) There was no allegation against the appellant that he was not in possession of any of the four registered letters. [410 D] (ii) The prosecution having merely showed that the registered articles were in the exclusive possession of the appellant, there was nothing wrong in the trial court convicting him. [411 A B] (iii) The prosecution has merely shown that these articles were planted by the opposite party. [412 E] (iv) The prosecution had merely shown that those articles were planted in the house. [413 F] (v) The prosecution did not show that the appellant knew that the articles were in his exclusive possession. The Commission also made an order that the case be referred to the Commission. The petitioner company filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the order of the Commission. 6778: The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court and Chief Justice of the High Court. He was appointed as a Judge of this Court by the President of India under Article 124(4) of the Constitution. The appellant challenged his appointment before the High Court on the ground that he had been removed from his office by an order passed by the President in exercise of the power conferred upon him by clause (c) of sub section 1 of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant could not be prosecuted for having committed the offence of criminal misconduct as contemplated by clause (e) of sub Section 1 of section5 of the Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence of civil contempt against a Judge of a High Court without the consent of the President and that the High court had no power to remove him from his office without the consent given by the President. HELD: (1) The High Court has no inherent power to punish a person for committing any criminal contempt of its own or of its own. [801 G] (2) The High Courts have inherent powers to punish a High Court Judge for criminal contempt of their own. The High Courts are vested with such powers which may be necessary for ensuring proper administration of justice in the country. The High courts have inherent powers under article 225 of the Constitution to punish a Judge for criminal Contempt of the High Courts. [802 A B] (3) The High court is not bound to follow the procedure laid down by the Code of Criminal Procedure for trial of cases instituted otherwise than on a police report. 415: The appellant was detained under the Bombay Police Act, 1951. 5538: The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. 652: The appellants and others were carrying on business in cotton and groundnut. They filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, as amended by the Madras General Sales Tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Act and the Rules constituted an unreasonable restriction upon the appellants ' fundamental right to carry on trade or business guaranteed under article 19(1)(g). [857 B] The Act and Rules are not invalid for the reason that they are inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in the Act. The Act and Rule 37 of the Rules are valid and constitutional. [858 C D] The Act does not provide for the grant of licences to persons who do business in cotton or groundnuts. It only provides for the regulation of buying and selling of commercial crops. The Act does no more than make provision for the regulation and control of the buying and selling by a market committee of agricultural produce and other commodities in respect of which it has authority to sell agricultural produce. Section 5(4)(a) of the Act makes it clear that the Act applies to all notified agricultural produce and agricultural produce. Therefore, the Act and Rules made thereunder are not violative of article 19(6) of the Constitution. [859 E F; 860 A B]

4807: The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti on an ad hoc basis. On April 2, 1975, he was appointed as an officiating Head Clerk in a substantive vacancy in the office of the Development Commissioner. On March 14, 1975, his services were terminated by the Panchayat Samiti. The appellant challenged the termination order before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion to the post of a Head Clerk from the date on which he was so appointed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant was not entitled to be treated as a permanent employee; (ii) since he had been working as a head clerk prior to his absorption in the Panchayat Samiti, he could not be treated as an ad hoc employee; (iii) since he was appointed lawfully to the post, he was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat Samiti until he was absorbed into the Panchayat; and (iv) since the appellant was promoted as an officiating head clerk, his appointment as a head clerks was valid. 3893: The appellant divorced her husband in 1965. She was living with her parents and a daughter. In the year 1967, she filed a suit for maintenance against her husband and his family members. The trial court decreed the suit on the footing that the appellant was a divorcee and awarded monthly allowance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for the mother for their subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay, where the parties lived, was high. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the courts below had erred in holding that the appellant had neglected to maintain herself and her child and that the respondent deserted her without any reasonable cause. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code is not exhaustive but only illustrative. It is open to the court to consider whether the applicant is a wife or a divorcee. [501 B] (2) The Explanation does not say that there must be proof of neglect to maintain the wife. The Explanation merely states that the wife may have to pay maintenance to the husband if he has sufficient means to pay such amount as she can afford to support herself. The Explanation does nothing more than emphasise that the expression 'wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. [504 C D] (3) The Explanation cannot be read as conferring upon the husband an absolute right to claim maintenance under section 127(3)(b). The Explanation does no more than elucidating the meaning of the word 'wife ' used in the Explanation. The Explanation is intended to provide a measure of social justice to women who are dependent on the income of the husband. The Explanation cannot therefore be construed as giving a wider meaning to the expression 'wife ' so as to include cases of divorce by mutual consent. [506 F H] (4) The Explanation is not exhaustive. It is designed to prevent the application of the provisions of the Act to cases of divorce between spouses by mutual consent, and to avoid hardship to spouses by applying the rule of harmonious construction.
